\chapter{Happy, bored, angry and sad}
\label{ch:ar-happy-bored-angry-and-sad}
\hlchaptermodality{488}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about happiness and boredom, and say that someone got angry, grieved or sighed.}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 488: I can talk about happiness and boredom, and say that someone got angry, grieved or sighed.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{سعادة} (saʿāda)}{سعادة (saʿāda)}]{\ar{سعادة} (saʿāda) — happiness}

\label{lesson:AR-C488-saada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a sentence, then the Arabic for a barber.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{سعادة}}
\textbf{\ar{سعادة}} — \emph{saʿāda} — \textquotedblleft{}happiness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{شعرت} \ar{بسعادة} \ar{كبيرة} \ar{في} \ar{العيد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{shaʿartu bi-saʿāda kabīra fī al-ʿīd.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
I felt great happiness at the feast.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{سعادة}} (\emph{saʿāda}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{s-a-d}, \textquotedblleft{}to be lucky, to be happy\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Saʿāda is the state of being saʿīd, happy, a word you already know from the same root.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{saʿāda}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{saʿāda}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shaʿartu bi-saʿāda kabīra fī al-ʿīd.} — I felt great happiness at the feast.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a sentence, then the Arabic for a barber, then say \emph{saʿāda} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{سعادة} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Happiness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{ملل} (malal)}{ملل (malal)}]{\ar{ملل} (malal) — boredom}

\label{lesson:AR-C488-malal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a barber, then the Arabic for happiness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{ملل}}
\textbf{\ar{ملل}} — \emph{malal} — \textquotedblleft{}boredom\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{شعر} \ar{الطالب} \ar{بالملل} \ar{في} \ar{المحاضرة} \ar{الطويلة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{shaʿara aṭ-ṭālib bi-l-malal fī al-muḥāḍara aṭ-ṭawīla.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The student felt bored in the long lecture.
\end{quote}

Arabic says \ar{شعر} \ar{بالملل}, to feel boredom, where English says to be bored.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{ملل}} (\emph{malal}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{m-l-l}, \textquotedblleft{}to be weary of a thing\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Malal is the noun of that weariness.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{malal}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{malal}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shaʿara aṭ-ṭālib bi-l-malal fī al-muḥāḍara aṭ-ṭawīla.} — The student felt bored in the long lecture.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a barber, then the Arabic for happiness, then say \emph{malal} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{ملل} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Boredom\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{غضب} (ghaḍiba)}{غضب (ghaḍiba)}]{\ar{غضب} (ghaḍiba) — to get angry}

\label{lesson:AR-C488-ghadiba}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for happiness, then the Arabic for boredom.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{غضب}}
\textbf{\ar{غضب}} — \emph{ghaḍiba} — \textquotedblleft{}to get angry\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{غضب} \ar{أبي} \ar{لأن} \ar{أخي} \ar{كسر} \ar{النافذة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ghaḍiba abī li-anna akhī kasara an-nāfidha.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My father got angry because my brother broke the window.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يغضب}, \emph{yaghḍab}.

It takes \ar{من} for the person: \ar{غضب} \ar{من} \ar{أخيه}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{غضب}} (\emph{ghaḍiba}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{gh-ḍ-b}, \textquotedblleft{}anger, wrath\textquotedblright{} (Lane). The adjective ghāḍib, angry, and the noun ghaḍab, anger, come from the same root.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghaḍiba}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghaḍiba}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghaḍiba abī li-anna akhī kasara an-nāfidha.} — My father got angry because my brother broke the window.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for happiness, then the Arabic for boredom, then say \emph{ghaḍiba} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{غضب} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To get angry\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{حزن} (ḥazina)}{حزن (ḥazina)}]{\ar{حزن} (ḥazina) — to grieve, to be sad}

\label{lesson:AR-C488-hazina}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for boredom, then the Arabic for to get angry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{حزن}}
\textbf{\ar{حزن}} — \emph{ḥazina} — \textquotedblleft{}to grieve, to be sad\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{حزنت} \ar{البنت} \ar{عندما} \ar{سافرت} \ar{صديقتها}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ḥazinat al-bint ʿindamā sāfarat ṣadīqatuhā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The girl was sad when her friend went away.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يحزن}, \emph{yaḥzan}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{حزن}} (\emph{ḥazina}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ḥ-z-n}, \textquotedblleft{}grief, sadness\textquotedblright{} (Lane). The adjective ḥazīn, sad, which you already know, comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ḥazina}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ḥazina}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ḥazinat al-bint ʿindamā sāfarat ṣadīqatuhā.} — The girl was sad when her friend went away.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for boredom, then the Arabic for to get angry, then say \emph{ḥazina} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{حزن} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To grieve, to be sad\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{تنهد} (tanahhada)}{تنهد (tanahhada)}]{\ar{تنهد} (tanahhada) — to sigh}

\label{lesson:AR-C488-tanahhada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to get angry, then the Arabic for to grieve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{تنهد}}
\textbf{\ar{تنهد}} — \emph{tanahhada} — \textquotedblleft{}to sigh\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{تنهدت} \ar{أمي} \ar{وجلست} \ar{على} \ar{الكرسي}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{tanahhadat ummī wa-jalasat ʿalā al-kursī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My mother sighed and sat down on the chair.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يتنهد}, \emph{yatanahhad}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{تنهد}} (\emph{tanahhada}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{n-h-d}, \textquotedblleft{}to swell, to rise\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives Form V tanahhada as to sigh: to let the chest rise with a long breath.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tanahhada}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tanahhada}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tanahhadat ummī wa-jalasat ʿalā al-kursī.} — My mother sighed and sat down on the chair.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to get angry, then the Arabic for to grieve, then say \emph{tanahhada} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{تنهد} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To sigh\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
